analysis.one_liner: Caps the money credit reporting agencies must pay consumers for violating credit accuracy laws.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill 27-23 on June 30, 2026; the full House and Senate have not voted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Credit Reporting Act lets consumers sue credit bureaus and companies that report inaccurate credit information. Courts can order unlimited punitive damages for willful violations, and class actions can win large total recoveries. This bill caps punitive-type damages, caps total class recovery at $500,000 or 1% of the company's net worth, and caps attorneys' fees and court costs.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumer credit reporting agencies (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion and their peers) and companies that furnish credit data, which face far smaller payouts when they willfully or negligently violate the law. Supporters say this also curbs lawsuits over small technical errors and reduces costs that get passed on to consumers through credit prices.

how_it_helps.text: For willful noncompliance, it eliminates courts' ability to award unlimited punitive damages and caps additional damages at the lesser of $100,000 or 40% of actual damages [S2][S3].
In class actions, it bars courts from applying a minimum per-member damages amount and caps the class's total recovery at the lesser of $500,000 or 1% of the defendant's net worth [S2][S3].
It caps the class's costs and attorney fees at the lesser of $100,000 or 40% of damages awarded, limiting the financial incentive for lawyers to take these cases [S2][S3].
For negligent noncompliance, it caps additional damages at the lesser of $100,000 or 40% of actual damages, and applies similar caps to negligent class actions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers harmed by wrong credit reports — people denied loans, jobs, or housing because of inaccurate or mixed-up credit files. Their recoveries would be capped, and in large class actions the total cap could cover only a small fraction of the harm. Plaintiffs' attorneys, whose fee caps reduce the incentive to take these cases, also bear a cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers suing over credit report errors

drawbacks.text: Money damages are the main practical remedy under the Fair Credit Reporting Act; the bill caps punitive damages, class-wide recovery at $500,000 or 1% of net worth, and attorney fees, which could make most violations unprofitable to sue over and leave inaccurate records in place [S2][S3].

In a large data breach or mass error affecting millions of consumers, a $500,000 class cap works out to pennies per person, and consumers with small actual damages would have almost no remedy once the minimum per-member damages rule is barred [S2][S3].
Fee caps of $100,000 or 40% of damages could mean attorneys cannot afford to litigate complex cases against large agencies, shrinking enforcement to cases with big provable losses only [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters' best argument is that unlimited punitive and statutory damages punish technical violations out of proportion to actual harm and that litigation costs get baked into credit prices for everyone. But the caps are blunt: the same $500,000 class limit that stops a wildly disproportionate judgment also guts recovery for genuine mass errors, and fee caps make small-dollar harms effectively unsuable. The bill trades the removal of real deterrence for industry cost savings, and consumers with the least provable damage lose the most.

outcome.mechanism: The House Financial Services Committee approved an amended version on a narrow 27-23 vote in June 2026, and the bill now sits waiting for a vote by the full House, which has not scheduled one; the Senate has not acted.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced October 17, 2025 by Rep. Loudermilk with five original cosponsors and referred to the Financial Services and Judiciary Committees [S1][S3][S5].
It gathered 7 cosponsors, all Republicans; no Democrat signed on [S4].
On June 30, 2026, the Financial Services Committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported in amended form by a vote of 27 to 23 [S5].
The full House has not voted, and there is no Senate action in the record; Congress remains in session [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the consumer credit reporting industry, which moved one step closer to caps on its legal exposure while consumers' ability to recover for inaccurate credit records remains unchanged — but could shrink if the bill becomes law.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 7 cosponsors are Republicans, and the committee advanced it on a narrow 27-23 vote; the provided record does not include a party breakdown of that vote.

industries.note: The bill directly caps what these companies must pay for willful and negligent FCRA violations, including punitive damages and class-wide recoveries. Their legal exposure is the bill's sole target, and consumers' main remedy for wrong credit files is that same liability.

industries.industry: Banks, lenders, and other data furnishers
industries.note: Companies that furnish credit data can be liable under the FCRA for inaccurate reporting; the caps reduce their class action exposure too. Their savings come at the cost of weaker deterrence against reporting errors that hurt consumers.

industries.industry: Consumer attorneys and class action plaintiffs' bar
industries.note: Fee caps of $100,000 or 40% of damages, plus the ban on minimum per-member class damages, cut the economics of taking FCRA cases. Their loss tracks directly with consumers losing a practical enforcement channel.

analysis.trajectory: The bill cleared committee on a narrow, essentially one-party vote with no Democratic cosponsors. It must now win a full House floor vote and pass the Senate, which has not acted on any version; consumer liability caps of this kind typically stall without broader bipartisan support, so the likely path is that it remains pending or dies at the end of the Congress.
